soil-class-119.title: Andosols, the dark soils of volcanic ash
soil-class-119.text: Wet rice grown on the Andosols of Java feeds some of the world's densest populations. Andosols are soils formed in volcanic ash and other tephra, rich in allophane or in complexes of aluminum and organic matter. The name comes from Japanese an, 'dark', and do, 'soil', and it is a synonym of kuroboku. They develop in glass-rich parent material. While much volcanic glass remains they are called Vitric, and as the glass weathers they gain andic properties. The path depends on the ash and the climate. Acidic tephra in humid climates yields aluminum-organic complexes, giving Aluandic Andosols. Basic tephra or dry climates yield allophane and imogolite, giving Silandic Andosols. Both kinds hold much ferrihydrite and have a bulk density of 0.9 kg/dm3 or less. Silandic Andosols are very fertile unless phosphorus is fixed, bound so tightly that plants cannot use it. Andosols cover about 1–2% of Earth's ice-free land, mostly around the Pacific Ring of Fire, from Chile and Mexico to Japan, Java and New Zealand. In USDA soil taxonomy many are Andisols, though some fall in the Inceptisols. The type is also very old. Fossil Andosols far from today's volcanoes have been dated as far back as the Precambrian, 1.5 billion years ago.

soil-class-144.title: Stagnosols, soils waterlogged from above
soil-class-144.text: Stagnosols get wet from the top down. Surface water stagnates in them, and the redox processes it drives leave strong mottling, without a marked change in texture. Periodically wet, they are mottled in topsoil and subsoil, sometimes with concretions or a fully bleached albic topsoil. Many national systems call them pseudogley. They cover 150–200 million hectares, mostly on flat to gently sloping land in humid temperate West and Central Europe, North America, south-east Australia and Argentina. Water stagnating above a dense subsoil starves roots of oxygen. Unlike Gleysols they often need deep loosening or ploughing, not just drains, and once drained they can be fertile. Many are Aqualfs, Aquults, Aquents, Aquepts or Aquolls in USDA soil taxonomy.

soil-class-136.title: Planosols, sandy topsoil on a clay floor
soil-class-136.text: A Planosol changes abruptly from one layer to the next. A pale, coarse-textured topsoil sits directly on a dense, slowly permeable, much more clayey subsoil. The sharp break comes from layered deposits, or from clay being destroyed and removed. Water perches above it, creating temporary reducing conditions and a stagnic color pattern. Planosols cover about 130 million hectares of seasonally waterlogged flats in subtropical and temperate regions with marked wet and dry seasons. Oxygen shortage when wet, the dense subsoil and sometimes toxic aluminum hamper roots. Most are grazed and yields stay modest, though Southeast Asia grows paddy rice on them. The 1938 US classification already used the name; USDA soil taxonomy now puts most in the Albaqualfs, Albaquults and Argialbolls.

soil-class-135.title: Phaeozems, dark prairie soils without lime
soil-class-135.text: Phaeozems are dark soils with a high base status, much like Chernozems, but with no secondary carbonates within one meter of the surface. They form on loess and glacial till under humid and sub-humid tall-grass steppe. Extensive areas lie in the United States, Argentina and China. They typically hold about 5% organic matter and have a pH of 5–7. Farmers use them intensively for wheat, soybean and cotton and as improved cattle pasture. Most Phaeozems match the Udolls, a suborder of the Mollisols in USDA soil taxonomy.

soil-class-130.title: Kastanozems, the chestnut soils of dry grasslands
soil-class-130.text: Kastanozems are named for the chestnut, from the Russian and Latin words for it, after the color of its husk. Also called chestnut soils, they have a dark, humus-rich topsoil and secondary carbonates, yet they are paler than Chernozems. Native grassland gave them a brown surface layer within the first meter. They hold a high level of exchangeable calcium, and their secondary carbonates start within 70 cm of the mineral surface. They occupy relatively dry zones receiving 200 to 450 mm of rain a year. In USDA soil taxonomy they relate to the Mollisols.

soil-class-132.title: Lixisols, weathered tropical soils that keep their bases
soil-class-132.text: Lixisols are hard-weathered tropical soils that still keep their bases. They develop under intense tropical weathering in subhumid to semi-arid climates. Low-activity clays build up below the surface, and base saturation stays high: base cations equal or exceed exchangeable aluminum. With Acrisols they are the FAO groups of tropical climates with clay-enriched layers. In Amazonia they are among the natural soils too poor in minerals to resupply nutrients. Most USDA Alfisols are Luvisols or Lixisols in the WRB.

soil-class-149.title: Plaggen soils, built one sod at a time
soil-class-149.text: Farmers in north-west Europe built their own soil, one sod at a time, from the Middle Ages on. They cut sods of heath or grass with roots and humus, and used them as bedding for cattle or sheep. In spring they spread the slurry-soaked bedding on their fields as manure. Centuries of this turned poor Podzols into plaggen soil, a deep, humus-rich plaggic Anthrosol 40 cm to over 1.50 m deep. Modern arable soils reach about 30 cm. The fields rose with sharp edges, called Plaggenesche in Germany or Es in Dutch. The practice ended around 1900 with the arrival of fertilizers. Orkney had such soils by the 12th to 13th centuries, and parts of Shetland kept the method until the 1960s. Far away, Maori farmers in New Zealand used plaggen-like practices to improve drainage for kumara.

soil-class-134.title: Nitisols, deep red soils with shiny clods
soil-class-134.text: Break a Nitisol and its blocky clods show shiny pressure faces, shaped by iron oxides and high water content. Nitisols are deep, red, well-drained tropical soils with at least 30% clay and a strong polyhedral or blocky structure. The clay-rich layer extends as deep as 150 cm. They form from fine material weathered from intermediate to basic rock. Kaolinite, halloysite and iron oxides dominate, and they fix phosphorus. They occur in the tropics and subtropics, extensively in the highlands of Ethiopia, Kenya, the DR Congo and Cameroon. They correlate with kandic Alfisols, Ultisols and Inceptisols of USDA soil taxonomy.

soil-class-146.title: Umbrisols, dark topsoils poor in bases
soil-class-146.text: An Umbrisol has a dark, organic-rich mineral topsoil, yet its base saturation is low. That makes it the low-base counterpart of Chernozems, Kastanozems and Phaeozems. It develops in weathered siliceous rock. Umbrisols cover about 100 million hectares. They lie above the tree line in the Andes, Himalaya and Central Asia, and lower down in cleared northern and western Europe and on North America's Pacific seaboard. Slopes and a wet, cool climate restrict most to extensive grazing, improved by better grasses and lime, and many erode easily. In New Zealand they became productive sheep and dairy land. USDA soil taxonomy places such soils in great groups of Entisols and Inceptisols. The British soils described in {{ref:soil-class-049}} are Umbrisols in the WRB.

soil-class-140.title: Retisols, where pale soil reaches down in a net
soil-class-140.text: In a Retisol, pale soil reaches down into the darker layer below in a net-like pattern. The pale part is a clay-poor eluvial horizon; the dark part is the clay-rich argic horizon. The interfingering is called retic properties, from Latin rete, 'net'. Retisols entered the WRB in its third edition in 2014, absorbing the more narrowly defined {{ref:soil-class-147}} of 1998 and 2006. They resemble the FAO's Podzoluvisols. They occur mainly in former periglacial areas of the last glaciation in Europe and North America, along a belt from Belgium to Russia, though rarely over large areas. Water drains through the clay-poor tongues. The dense, nutrient-richer clay parts are often too dry and hard for roots, and earthworms avoid them. Most Retisols are forest or pasture.

soil-class-150.title: The Black Dirt Region, onion country on drained muck
soil-class-150.text: By the late 20th century, onions on this ground averaged 30,000 lb/acre (3.4 kg/m2). The Black Dirt Region is a drained former marsh in Orange County, New York, and Sussex County, New Jersey. It is named for its dark, extremely fertile {{ref:soil-class-109}} muck. The muck formed on an ancient glacial lake bed, enriched by decades of Wallkill River floods. Its 26,000 acres (10,400 ha) are the largest such tract in the US outside the Everglades. Early settlers avoided the flood-prone land. A drainage canal was dug in 1835, and Polish and Volga German immigrants used to similar soils began farming it. Farmers now also grow vegetables, sod, hemp and cannabis. The muck is poor ground for building, so development of the farmland is considered unlikely.

soil-class-137.title: Plinthosols, soils that can harden into ironstone
soil-class-137.text: Some tropical soils can turn to stone. Plinthite, a red, clay-rich material rich in iron oxides, sometimes over 80%, hardens irreversibly into ironstone with repeated wetting and drying. Plinthosols are defined by plinthite, petroplinthite or pisoliths, iron-oxide concretions, in a plinthic horizon starting within 50 cm of the surface. They form in wet-dry tropics where water tables rise and fall. Saturated soil reduces and mobilizes iron, which precipitates as ferric oxides in mottled patterns when the soil dries. Fertility is low. Bottomlands waterlog, shallow areas suffer drought, and shallow petroplinthite often leaves only grazing, though cocoa and cashew are grown in places. Soils with plinthite cover about 60 million hectares. Soft plinthite dominates the humid Amazon and Congo basins, while hardened caps cover drier Sudano-Sahelian landforms.

soil-class-129.title: Gypsisols, gypsum soils of the driest lands
soil-class-129.text: Water can make a Gypsisol sink. These soils hold a substantial secondary accumulation of gypsum (CaSO4·2H2O) and are confined to the driest arid lands. Probably about 100 million hectares in all, they lie around Mesopotamia, central Asia, the Libyan and Namib deserts, Australia and the south-western United States. Calcium sulfate, with or without carbonates, collects in and below the B horizon of soils formed in alluvial, colluvial and wind-blown deposits. Deep Gypsisols near water can grow many crops, but a shallow petrogypsic horizon cuts yields. Gypsum dissolving in irrigation water makes the land subside unevenly, so canals must be lined. They are Gypsids in USDA soil taxonomy and Desert soils in the Russian classification.

soil-class-125.title: Durisols, dryland soils cemented by silica
soil-class-125.text: Durisol comes from Latin durus, 'hard', and the name fits. In these free-draining dryland soils, secondary silica cements the grains in the upper meter, as nodules or as a continuous hardpan. The cemented layer is called a duripan, hardpan in Australia or dorbank in South Africa. Durisols form mainly in alluvial and colluvial deposits on plains, terraces and gentle piedmont slopes in arid, semi-arid and Mediterranean regions. Erosion often exposes the hard layer. Most are fit only for extensive grazing; crops need irrigation. Large areas occur in Australia, South Africa, Namibia and the south-western United States. As a new group, though, they are rarely mapped, and their extent is unknown.

soil-class-124.title: Why chernozem is black: an open question
soil-class-124.text: How chernozem got its thick black topsoil has been argued since 1763. That year Lomonosov pointed to decaying plants and animals. Murchison proposed weathered Jurassic marine shales in 1840, others marine sediments in 1851, and Ruprecht decomposed steppe grasses in 1866. The puzzle is still open. No single reconstruction of past climate explains the geochemical variation of central European chernozems. Evidence of human-made pyrogenic carbon, carbon formed by burning, led to a burning theory from Schmidt in 1999. Chernozem has the highest magnetic susceptibility of the major soil types. Heat turns goethite and ferrihydrite into maghemite, which points to fire, likely set by early humans. Yet humification alone can darken soils. So 'chernozem' may cover black soils that look alike but formed in different ways, and no single explanation yet fits them all.

soil-class-141.title: Five groups with clay-rich subsoils, and how to tell them apart
soil-class-141.text: Five WRB groups must have an argic horizon, a clay-enriched subsoil: Retisols, Acrisols, Lixisols, Alisols and Luvisols. The key sorts them with a few measurements. Retisols stand apart first, as the only group with retic properties. The other four are separated by the cation exchange capacity per kg of clay in the argic horizon, and by the effective base saturation of the subsoil. Low-activity clays with more exchangeable aluminum than base cations make an Acrisol. Low-activity clays with base cations at least equal to aluminum make a Lixisol. High-activity clays dominated by aluminum make an Alisol. High-activity clays with base cations at least equal to aluminum make a Luvisol. One exception guards the edge. A soil with an argic horizon and retic properties dominated by stagnant water is classed instead as a Retic Stagnosol. The groups also map onto the U.S. system. Most USDA Alfisols become Luvisols or Lixisols, and most Ultisols become Acrisols or Alisols.

soil-class-147.title: Albeluvisols, a soil group retired in 2014
soil-class-147.text: Albeluvisols lasted just two editions of the WRB, in 1998 and 2006. The group held soils with a thin dark topsoil over a bleached albic horizon that tongues into a clay-enriched Bt horizon. The third edition, in 2014, replaced them with the more broadly defined Retisols. They formed in glacial till, lake and river deposits or loess on plains under coniferous or mixed forest. They cover an estimated 320 million hectares, mostly on former Pleistocene permafrost. Acidity, few nutrients and problems with ploughing and drainage limit farming, so those of the northern taiga are almost all forest. They correlate with the Glossaqualfs, Glossocryalfs and Glossudalfs of USDA soil taxonomy.

reviews.world-reference-base-soil-groups: The soil groups of this chapter read like a record of the forces that make soil. Water sorts many of them: rising groundwater makes Gleysols, stagnant surface water makes Stagnosols and Planosols, and water washing clay downward builds the argic subsoils of Luvisols, Acrisols, Lixisols, Alisols and Retisols. Dry climates leave salts, lime, gypsum or silica behind, in Solonchaks, Calcisols, Gypsisols and Durisols. Dark, humus-rich topsoils mark Chernozems, Kastanozems and Phaeozems, though how the Chernozem's black layer formed is still debated, while Fluvisols, Leptosols, Regosols and Cambisols show soil formation barely begun. People leave their mark too, from the plaggen fields of north-west Europe to the landfills and mine spoil of Technosols.
